mainEntity.name: Can I get a payment gateway without a website?

acceptedAnswer.text: A payment gateway is built for a website and connects to your domain. Some facilitators also offer payment links, which help with the odd DM sale, but a payment link is not a website: no basket, no order history, no customer list.

mainEntity.name: How long does getting the trust symbol take?

acceptedAnswer.text: It depends on how complete your documents are. If your business details, address and site are ready and correct, the review usually takes a few working days. What slows it down is incomplete documents, and a site with no contact details or rules.

mainEntity.name: Is a payment facilitator safe, or must I take a direct bank gateway?

acceptedAnswer.text: Licensed facilitators operate under Shaparak, and your customer’s payment happens on a secure bank page, with the money settling into your own account. When you choose one, check the facilitator’s license and track record, and steer clear of unnamed intermediaries.

mainEntity.name: How much of my sales do gateway fees take?

acceptedAnswer.text: A direct bank gateway has lower, flatter fees, while facilitators take a percentage of each transaction. The exact figure depends on the bank and the facilitator, and it is published in their own tariffs. Check there, against your sales volume, and work out which is worth more to you.

Payments and trust
Payment gateway and trust symbol: how your shop starts taking real money

While your money still moves by card transfers and screenshot receipts, your shop has a ceiling. Every order is a chat. Every payment is a worry. A payment gateway and a trust symbol are the two pieces that turn an Instagram shop into a real store.
25 November 2026·8 min read·The dadmor team

In this article

  1. Why card to card transfers put a ceiling on your shop
  2. What a payment gateway actually is, and the two ways to get one
  3. What the trust symbol (eNAMAD) is, and how to get it
  4. The checklist to finish on your site before you apply
  5. What actually changes once the gateway is connected?
  6. The bottom line

Summary

  1. A payment gateway means your customer pays inside your site, right then, and the order registers itself. No more chats asking for a card number. No receipts to check by hand.
  2. You have two routes: a direct bank gateway, which asks for the trust symbol and a tax tracking code, and a payment facilitator, which starts with simpler verification. The trust symbol itself comes from the eNAMAD system.
  3. Before you apply, get your site ready: real contact details, buying and returns rules, a privacy page, and correct prices and stock. They look at your site first. Then they grant the symbol and the gateway.

An order lands in your DMs. You send a card number. The customer sends a screenshot of a receipt. You check the receipt against your balance, and only then, if it is not fake, you register the order. That loop just about works at ten orders a day. At fifty, it is one full time person doing nothing but checking receipts.

An online payment gateway kills that loop. Put plainly, it is the secure page where your customer pays by card inside your site, and the order registers itself. The trust symbol is the badge that tells the customer, and the bank, that this shop is real, with a known owner and address. Together they are the plumbing of real selling, not decoration.

We will go in order: what each one is, where you get it, and what to prepare before you apply. One honest note up front: neither happens in a day, and neither happens without documents. But the path is clear, and you only walk it once.
Why card to card transfers put a ceiling on your shop
Card to card is fine when you are starting out. It has three problems, though, and all three grow as your shop grows:

items: Fake receipts and manual checking: every receipt has to be checked against your account, and fake receipts are not rare. Get one wrong and the goods have left while the money never arrived.

Customers who abandon halfway: when a buyer sees they have to leave your site, open a banking app and transfer money by hand, many drop the purchase right there. Paying inside the site is one step. A manual transfer is five.

A personal account and messy books: heavy traffic through a personal account raises questions at the bank, and it mixes your shop’s money with household spending. Come the end of the month, you cannot tell what you actually sold.

blocks.html: A payment gateway solves all three at once. The money lands in your business account, traceable, and every payment is tied to one specific order.
What a payment gateway actually is, and the two ways to get one

A payment gateway is a secure page that a bank, or an intermediary company, puts at your site’s disposal. Your customer pays there with their own card. The result, success or failure, comes back to your site, and the order registers. There are two ways to get one:

items: Direct bank gateway: you take it from the bank itself. It needs the trust symbol, a tax tracking code and a business bank account. Fees are lower, but setup takes more documents and more time.

Payment facilitator: these are companies working under Shaparak, the national payment network, and they hand you a ready made gateway. You start with identity verification and a live website, and usually you do not need the trust symbol on day one. In return, they take a percentage fee on each transaction.

blocks.html: Our honest take: if your site is new and you want to start selling quickly, a facilitator is the easier start. Once sales are steady and you have the symbol, add a direct gateway beside it. Plenty of shops keep both, so if one goes down, selling does not stop.
A payment gateway means your customer pays in the same place they shopped. Every extra step between the basket and the payment is one more place to lose them for good.
What the trust symbol (eNAMAD) is, and how to get it

The electronic trust symbol, known as eNAMAD, is a badge that Iran’s E-Commerce Development Center grants to online shops after checking the owner’s identity and address. When a customer clicks the symbol on your site, they see your registered shop details. The steps are:

items: Register in the eNAMAD system: at enamad.ir you create an account and enter your business details, your site’s domain, your address and how customers can reach you.
Identity and address verification: the business owner’s identity documents and postal address get checked. This is why the address and phone on your site have to be real, and answered.
Site review: a reviewer goes through your site: contact details, buying and returns rules, and whether the shop is genuinely active and selling.
Place the symbol code: after approval, you put the symbol code on your site, usually in the footer, so a customer can pull up your details in one click.

blocks.html: The symbol has levels, and most shops start at the base level. The point that matters more: the symbol is issued for your own domain, so first you need a website of your own. In Shop builder or your own website we explain why that ownership matters more than renting space on someone else’s platform.
The checklist to finish on your site before you apply
For both the symbol and the gateway, your site gets reviewed first. Finish these before you apply, so nothing stalls in review:

items: Real contact details: an address, a phone that gets answered and an email, on the contact page and in the footer.
A rules page: buying terms, shipping cost and time, and the returns and exchange policy, written clearly, with no room for guessing.
A privacy page: what you do with customer information, and who can get to it.
Correct prices and stock: a sold out product should not still be sellable, and prices should be up to date.
A live site on the exact domain you register for the symbol. The symbol is tied to that domain.

blocks.html: If you do not have a site yet, or yours is missing these basics, fix that first. On our website building page we list what a complete shop site includes, and with the project estimator you can see what setting one up costs before you decide anything.
What actually changes once the gateway is connected?

items: Orders register themselves: a successful payment becomes an order in your panel, with the customer’s details attached. No DM orders. No manual receipts.
Money is traceable: every transaction carries a tracking code, and refunds go back to the customer through the same path, documented. No pleading card transfers.
Trust at the moment of payment: a clickable trust symbol and a bank payment page the customer recognises. They matter most exactly there, where a stranger is about to pay you for the first time.

blocks.html: And one honest boundary: a gateway and a symbol do not sell anything on their own. They remove the friction at payment. Bringing the customer in, and convincing them, is still the work of product and content. In Traffic but no sales we list the places to check between a customer arriving and a customer buying.
The bottom line

The whole path looks like this: your own site, with complete details and rules. The trust symbol from eNAMAD. Then a payment gateway, direct or through a facilitator. You do each step once, and after that your shop runs on rails: the customer arrives, pays, and the order registers, without you standing in the middle of every purchase checking receipts.
Is your site ready for a gateway?

The first step is a site that a gateway and a symbol can actually sit on: real contact details, clear rules, a working basket. The project estimator shows you the cost and time of building one in a few minutes, and the website building page shows what a complete shop includes.
Frequently asked questions

Can I get a payment gateway without a website?

A payment gateway is built for a website and connects to your domain. Some facilitators also offer payment links, which help with the odd DM sale, but a payment link is not a website: no basket, no order history, no customer list.
